::: {.lead-serif}
Three questions run through my work: who governs speech technology, how to build it for languages with little data, and how people and machines read meaning beyond the words.

## Speech technology ethics {#ethics}

Speech technology now decides who gets heard in public agencies, classrooms and courts, but the law governing it assumes a single claimant with a grievance. When a system fails a language, it fails everyone who speaks it. I work on that gap: fairness and bias, consent over speech data, and the standing of language communities under AI law and minority-language instruments. Frisian is the recurring test case.

## AI for small data {#small-data}

Most of the world's languages have little recorded speech, and the systems in widest use simply skip them. We build speech recognition and synthesis that work from small amounts of data, using multilingual and cross-lingual transfer, data augmentation and evaluation methods designed for low-resource settings. Frisian, Bildts and Luxembourgish are current cases.

The linguistic groundwork comes from years of fieldwork on Aymara and other Andean languages: a reference grammar, studies of its phonology and verbal art, and an early rule-based machine translation system.

## Meaning beyond words {#meaning}

Speech carries more than words: emotion, intent, irony. Sarcasm is our central test case, since speakers routinely mean the opposite of what they say. We combine acoustic, linguistic and visual cues to detect it, and we synthesize it to find out which cues listeners actually use. Related work looks at how listeners perceive prosody, including through cochlear implants and in Parkinson's speech, and at how people experience sound in everyday places.
